Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette:
Letao was sixty-three, a financial analyst who had spent decades reading spreadsheets in a quiet office, when a delivery truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at an intersection two miles from home. The crash itself took seconds: the screech of tires, the explosive crumple of metal, the smell of gasoline and hot rubber flooding the cabin as the car spun and came to rest against a light pole. He was not badly injured-a cracked rib, bruises-but in the moments after impact, pinned by the seatbelt in the dark, smoke-filled space, he had been certain he was about to die. The darkness pressed in, and the sound of the other vehicle's engine, still running and whining, played over and over in his ears.

In the months that followed, Letao found he could not shake the feeling that the event was still happening. A sudden car sound on the street-a backfire, a horn-would instantly return the full memory without warning: the smell of gasoline, the sensation of the car still spinning, the auditory replay of that grinding engine noise in his head. The memory felt present, not past, as though he were again trapped in the dark. He began to notice that his body reacted before his mind had time to think; his shoulders would tense, his breathing would quicken, and he would be scanning for exits the moment he entered any room, even his own kitchen. He woke during the night to check whether he was safe, lying still and listening for sounds that did not belong.

Letao had come to believe that he had to be on guard all the time. He told himself that if he let his mind dwell on the crash, even for a moment, he would not be able to handle it-the fear would overwhelm him completely. So he avoided thinking about it, but the vigilance itself became exhausting. Because he was certain that you never knew what could happen next, he started driving only on familiar roads during daylight, and he began to leave every meeting early so he could be home before dusk. The smell of gasoline at a service station became unbearable; he would cross the street to avoid it, and on days when the wind carried it toward him, he felt the old dread surge. The darkness of his own garage at night began to feel threatening, and he would flip the light switch before stepping inside, his heart already pounding.

The more he watched for danger, the more he found it. His hypervigilance meant that a car door slamming in the parking lot could trigger the memory again, and the memory, in turn, reinforced his belief that the world was unsafe. He became convinced that he needed to be especially careful, which only heightened his bodily alertness. The loop tightened over weeks and months: he would wake alert, checking for threats, and the silence of the house would somehow remind him of the quiet after the crash, bringing the memory flooding back. At work, his concentration frayed. He began to avoid the windowed conference room because its street view let him hear traffic; he moved his desk to an interior cubicle. His supervisor noticed that he was leaving early and missing deadlines, but Letao could not explain why. He was certain that if he told anyone about the fear, they would think he was broken.

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife's quiet observation that he had not sat with her in the living room after dark in four months. He wanted to, but the thought of the unlit room, the possibility of a car passing, the way his body would react before he could tell himself it was safe-it all felt unmanageable. He came to therapy hoping to stop the cycle, but what frightened him most was the possibility that the feeling of being in that car, in the dark, with the smell of gasoline, would never really end.
